newsitem.title: USA: Court rejects appeal that held up Texas executions.
newsitem.headline: Court rejects appeal that held up Texas executions.

text.p: A Texas appeals court upheld a state law Wednesday shortening the appeals process for death row inmates, clearing the way for executions to resume in the state, attorneys said.

The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals rejected a death row inmate's challenge to a 1995 law limiting condemned prisoners to one state appeal to a higher state or federal court and cutting legal-assistance funds for death row inmates.

Twenty one executions have been stayed in Texas since February, including eight involving inmates who joined convicted murderer James Carl Lee Davis in challenging the state's streamlined appeals process.

Davis, 32, has been on death row since March 1986 after he beat to death three children aged 4, 6 and 15 with a lead pipe and raped the 15-year old while burglarizing the home of his next-door neighbour.

"The district attorneys now can approach the trial courts to reschedule the executions," Sonya Sanchez, spokeswoman with the Texas Attorney General's office, said. "We will probably see executions resume on what Texas has seen as a normal schedule in about March."

Texas leads the nation in the number of executions since capital punishment resumed in 1982. But after carrying out a record 19 executions in 1995, only three people were sent to the death house in the state prison in Huntsville this year.

The decision by the highest criminal court in Texas follows a U.S. Supreme Court ruling in July upholding limits to federal habeas corpus appeals, which allow convicted felons to appeal a verdict to a higher state or federal court.
In Texas, 448 people are on death row, where inmates spend an average eight years appealing their convictions before executions are carried out.
